verdict.reasoning: The doctor states the patient is having 'some sort of lip swelling' and the patient links onset to eating 'a prawn soup.'
Patient says she had the prawn soup 'maybe like around seven' and the swelling developed in 'half an hour maybe,' matching onset ~30 minutes after eating at ~19:00.
Patient reports lips started feeling weird 'just in the, in the corner, sort of on the left first' and later 'there is like a swelling on my upper lip and it's kind of getting bigger.'
Patient says 'you can still feel it, like really pumping blood and it's kind of getting bigger. It feels like it's getting worse,' matching a pumping sensation and increase in size.

Patient states 'I feel like I can't breathe that well' and when asked about chest tightness says 'Chest just generally feels a little difficult... it might be. I'm not sure,' indicating breathing difficulty and possible chest tightness.

Patient recalls 'like a year ago... I woke up the next morning quite swollen up and had also like... felt really bad and quite difficult breathing, but I don't know what it was. I had. It was like a curry or something.'
Patient clearly states 'I generally have asthma.'
Patient says 'I tell. I take. What's it called? Salbutamol inhalus... So I do take that regularly.'
Patient says she sometimes uses antihistamines but is unsure which ones: 'Sometimes, but I don't know which ones.' Later, when asked if she has any now, she answers 'No, I don't think I have.'
Patient states 'So I have a peanut allergy as well. Yeah, like always had it?'

Doctor asks if she ever used an injection and if she had to go to hospital; patient only recalls her mom told her about an injection and that she was about six, but details are unclear: 'I don't know what it was because I was small... Has your mom ever said that you had to go to hospital... Yeah, well, I was like six or something, I think...' The transcript does not clearly confirm both an injection and hospital care together as a severe reaction per mother’s report.
Initially patient is alone, then states 'Somebody just came... Yes, Mom.' indicating she is now with her mother at the scene.

Doctor says 'it sounds like you could be going into what we say, anaphylactic reaction... that's when your throat and your chest closes in,' in the context of acute upper lip swelling after prawn soup and reported breathing difficulty and chest discomfort.
Asthma is mentioned as past medical history, but the clinician does not explicitly state that asthma increases the risk or severity of the current reaction.

There is known peanut allergy ('So I have a peanut allergy as well'), and the doctor asks about injections; patient says 'my mom told me about it, but I don't know what it was,' making prior intramuscular epinephrine use unclear, consistent with IgE‑mediated food allergy and uncertain prior adrenaline use.

Doctor says 'I think we need to call an ambulance... hang on the line while I'll call the ambulance' and tells mom to 'call the 999... and say that there is a suspected anaphylactic reaction and they need to come straight away,' indicating EMS activation and urgent ED transport.

Doctor instructs, 'Could you ask the person whether they have any antihistamines around... So straight away, take the antihistamines in the meantime,' which is use of an oral antihistamine while awaiting EMS.

Doctor says 'Make sure that person's with you till the ambulance comes' and instructs mom to call 999 immediately; this covers staying with an escort and immediate emergency call if concern persists/worsens.
Doctor advises post-hospital follow-up for 'your injections and things like that,' but does not specifically mention an allergy service, adrenaline auto-injector, or full allergy workup.

Doctor states 'Come out from the hospital. Do give us a ring back. We might need to sort you out with your injections and things like that,' advising contact after ED visit for further management and arranging injections and education.
Follow-up is suggested ('Do give us a ring back'), but there is no explicit instruction that follow-up must be in a clinic or dedicated allergy service.
'Come out from the hospital. Do give us a ring back' directly instructs the patient to contact the service after the ED visit for further management.
The transcript contains no mention of vital signs (e.g., blood pressure, pulse, respiratory rate, temperature), so stating that none were recorded is consistent with the record.
